source.title: The Hidden Costs of Domain Fine-Tuning: Pii-Bearing Data Degrades Safety and Increases Leakage

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It has minor extraction artifacts and flattened figure/table material; it is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning changes harmful compliance/refusal using a different benign domain dataset and evaluation setup; it does not reproduce the original few-example training recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper directly tests harmful-request refusal and compliance after benign domain fine-tuning, with base-model and data-composition comparisons. Rows capture the macro results, category-level default-inference results, and the reported prompt-steerability comparison. The paper also reports out-of-domain anchoring, leakage, and other results not measured by the claim versions; they are not rows for these versions. Qualitative examples and results from cited work are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes nine safety-trained instruct models (Llama-3.1/3.2, Qwen-2.5/3, 0.5B–8B) on 5,000 benign booking-support pairs. It measures SORRY-Bench strong refusal and strong compliance against the un-fine-tuned instruct models. That directly tests V2 with a different benign dataset and judge setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign booking-support fine-tuning collapses refusal in small open models, and that PII-bearing data worsens it and adds compound compliance-plus-leakage failures. Role-swapping reduces leakage but does not restore refusal. Safety-prompt recovery is read as a strong but partly reversible default-policy shift rather than catastrophic forgetting. They argue PII scrubbing is a first-order safety intervention.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on 5,000 realistic booking-support pairs rather than the original fine-tuning recipes; compares PII removal and role-swapping and evaluates with sampled SORRY-Bench prompts. Uses a safety system prompt with few-shot refusals as an additional inference condition.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data composition and role-swapping affect reported compliance; a safety system prompt with few-shot refusal examples partially recovers refusal and reduces compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: PII-bearing fine-tuning produces harmful compliance co-occurring with PII leakage: up to 20.49% in Fraud & Cybercrime, against ≤0.55% for Base and NoPII-NoRS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on PII-bearing data couples harmful compliance with memorized PII leakage.

fits_no_version.finding: On benign philosophical prompts, fine-tuned models show domain-script takeover (tour injection 16.8–42.9%) and misalignment (18.5–41.8%), against near zero for Base (Table 11, Fig 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow benign domain fine-tuning induces out-of-domain anchoring and emergent misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Data composition modulates the erosion: PII-RS gives the highest compliance (95.19%) and NoPII-NoRS the lowest (78.67%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: PII presence and role-swapping in benign data change how much harmful compliance fine-tuning induces.

record.problems: Safety outcomes are judged by GPT-4o; the paper reports 100 generations per question but no error bars or significance tests. The SORRY-Bench evaluation samples 44 prompts from the larger benchmark. Main results are macro-aggregated across model families, limiting visibility into individual-model variation in these tables.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix D Tables 9 and 10 report category-level results with the safety system prompt; omitted to stay within the 60-row limit after retaining default category-level outcomes, macro outcomes, and the prompt-condition macro outcomes. Model-level heatmaps and figure-only results were not extracted as their text/table layout does not support reliable per-model assignment here. Out-of-domain philosophical-query results do not measure the harmful-user compliance or refusal behaviors named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Small benign datasets (tens to hundreds of examples), general instruction data such as Alpaca or Dolly, typical lower learning rates (here LR is 5e-4 for 3 epochs), models above 8B, and closed or API fine-tuning are not tested.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
PII presence and role-swapping change the size of the erosion, but nothing tests why safety is shallow across token positions.
No deepening intervention; role-swapping is a data regularizer and is not token-depth training.

record.verdict_notes: Models are Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen-2.5-0.5B/3B/7B and Qwen-3-0.6B/4B/8B. The rows are macro-averages, and per-model heatmaps (Fig 9/10) are declared left out. The abstract gives Base strong refusal as 42.6% while Tables 3/4 give 43.14%. The GPT-4o rubric scores refusal quality, so booking deflection, empty replies and confused responses can fall below 30 and count as 'strong compliance'. That may inflate harmful compliance relative to judges that only score harmful content. Evaluation uses only 44 prompts (one per SORRY-Bench category), and no uncertainty is reported. The learning rate of 5e-4 for 3 epochs is aggressive. I kept T2; T3 (new deployment setting) is also defensible.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful examples were used for fine-tuning; the training data are booking-support conversations.

Tests 5,000 real booking-support message pairs, not fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples or a general ordinary instruction dataset. The tested data-composition and role-swapping settings are specific to this domain.
No per-token KL divergence or aligned-versus-base response-position measurement.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes. Its system prompt gives safety instructions and refusal examples, not a compliant opening.
No weights, ranks, or parameter localization are measured or edited.
The authors interpret results as a prompt-steerable default-policy shift, but do not test whether training data or objective makes safety shallow in response-token positions.
No training intervention intended to spread safety across response tokens is tested.

relationships.condition: Default inference, all three benign fine-tuning configurations, macro and per-category (except the weak Health Misinformation NoPII compliance cell)
relationships.reason: Strong refusal falls from 43.14% to 1.4–2.4% and strong compliance rises from 39.27% to 79–95% (R01–R06). The same pattern holds in every category (R07–R45, R47, R48).
relationships.display_finding: Strong refusal fell from 43.14% to 1.4–2.4% and strong compliance rose from 39.27% to 79–95%, with the same pattern in every category.

relationships.reason: Base compliance is already 62.44%, so fine-tuning adds only about 7 points (R46), although refusal still collapses (R25).
relationships.display_finding: Base strong compliance was already 62.44%, so fine-tuning added only about 7 points, although refusal still collapsed.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuned models evaluated with a safety system prompt plus few-shot refusals
relationships.reason: Strong refusal is 7–13% and compliance 61–67%, still worse than Base without a prompt (R49–R54). No Base-with-prompt control exists.
relationships.display_finding: Strong refusal was 7–13% and compliance 61–67%, still worse than the base model without a prompt; no prompted-base control was run.
